summary.text: 干 is a whole-graph pictograph interpreted chiefly as a shield; early inscriptions also use it defensively. In simplified Chinese, it is also the spelling of the separate words traditionally written 乾 “dry” and 幹 “trunk.”

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph is interpreted chiefly as a shield, sometimes described as decorated with feathers. A shield reading is securely identified in a mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription; proposed Shang identifications remain disputed.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted chiefly as a shield, sometimes with feather decoration. A competing analysis treats some oracle-bone forms as variants of 單 depicting a forked hunting implement; this is an alternative reading of the whole graph, not a split into smaller components.

history.text: Some Shang forms have been proposed as 干, but that identification is disputed. The earliest securely identifiable example in this account is a mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription. Later Western Zhou forms regularize the forked top to a short horizontal stroke, retained in later scripts.

The Han-period Shuowen account analyzes 干 as 反入 plus 一 and gives it the sense “offend” or “violate.” This is a historical explanation of the graph and its meaning, distinct from the shield interpretation.

uncertainties.text: The shield interpretation has substantial scholarly support, but the identification of proposed Shang signs and the distinction between 干 and 盾 in some forms remain disputed. Another proposal treats some oracle-bone forms related to 單 as a forked hunting implement. The depicted object's ancient name and pronunciation are not established here.

The date and earlier spelling history of 干 as the simplified spelling of 乾 “dry” and 幹 “trunk” are unresolved here; these spellings do not establish derivation or semantic development from the shield sense.

senses.period: Securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou; proposed earlier Shang attribution is disputed.
senses.text: The graph is interpreted as a shield pictograph. A bronze inscription meaning “shield” is reported; the earliest secure attestation identified here is mid-Western Zhou.

senses.period: Early inscriptional and textual use reported; exact first date unresolved.
senses.text: A defensive or protective use is reported in an oracle-bone example and a later bronze inscription. Its relationship to the shield sense is not established.

senses.period: Recorded in a Han-period dictionary; date of the word sense unresolved.
senses.text: The Han-period Shuowen account gives “offend” or “violate” as a sense and analyzes the graph as 反入 plus 一. It does not explain how or when this sense arose.

senses.gloss: dry (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 乾)
senses.period: Current simplified spelling; the word sense’s onset is undated here.
senses.text: 干 is the current simplified spelling of 乾 for “dry.” The dry reading is recorded as gān, and its first-use date is unresolved. The Book of Odes passage is cited for the dry word written as 乾; 干 is its current simplified spelling. No semantic development from “shield” is established here.

senses.gloss: trunk; main stem (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 幹)
senses.period: Current simplified spelling; historical examples of 幹 do not date this spelling correspondence.
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 writes the word traditionally written 幹. Cited early examples of 幹 mean a tree stem or the body's frame; they do not show that this word developed from the shield sense.

limitations.text: The dry and trunk words are written 干 in simplified Chinese and 乾 and 幹, respectively, in traditional writing. The spelling chronology and any semantic transition from the shield word are not established here.
The historical dictionary explanation records the “offend/violate” sense but does not establish its chronology or development.

items.period: Received Shuowen seal-script style; modern vector redraw, uploaded 2007; not a dated artifact
items.caption: A received seal-style form of 干 has a tall central stroke crossing a broad horizontal stroke, with a curved, open upper section.
items.alt: Black seal-style 干 glyph with a long vertical stroke, a broad crossbar, and a curved forked top.
items.selection_reason: The visible redraw usefully shows the received seal-style form. It illustrates a later form, while the earliest secure attestation and the proposed earlier Shang forms have separate dating limits.
